question: The rise in the global average temperature due to climate change poses a serious risk to the health and safety of workers in Europe. An ACSH1 opinion highlights that exposure to high temperatures poses significant risks to the safety and health of workers, particularly in physically demanding jobs.

According to the International Labour Organization (ILO) and the European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC), deaths linked to high temperatures in workplaces in the EU have increased by 42 % since 2000, the fastest increase in occupational accidents worldwide2. Heat stress is now a structural occupational hazard, reducing productivity and increasing the need for breaks and the risk of errors and accidents at work.
Given that the current Directive3 has not been updated with specific provisions on heat stress: 1.
Does the Commission recognise occupational heat stress as a systemic risk factor for health and safety at work, requiring specific attention at EU level?

Does the Commission intend to respond to the trade unions' call for binding legislation on occupational exposure to high temperatures, with clear obligations for employers and specific protection for vulnerable groups of workers?

Opinion of the Advisory Committee on Safety and Health at Work, entitled ‘Climate Change – Heat at Work’ (https://circabc.europa.eu/ui/group/cb9293be-4563-4f19-89cf-4c4588bd6541/library/61e58999-6cfa-402d9d98-38fac4b2b001/details). https://www.etuc.org/en/document/content-directive-prevention-occupational-heat-risks. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EL/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:31989L0391.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.3.2026) The Commission considers that exposure to extreme temperatures at work is an important risk factor for workers’ occupational safety and health (OSH).

The EU OSH Framework Directive 89/391/EEC1 sets out the general obligations for employers, who are required to assess all risks at work, including those arising from exposure to high temperatures when workers are or can be exposed to such risks, and to take appropriate preventive and protective measures which shall take into account vulnerable workers.

A number of other EU OSH Directives include more detailed provisions with regard to temperature at work, such as the Workplace2, Construction Sites3, the Fishing Vessels4 and the two Extractive Industries Directives56.

For example, the Construction Directive specifies in its Annex IV that ’During working hours, the temperature must be appropriate for human beings, having regard to the working methods used and the physical demands placed on the workers’, and that ‘The temperature in rest areas, rooms for duty staff, sanitary facilities, canteens and first-aid rooms must be appropriate to the particular purpose of such areas’.

Similar provisions exist in the other mentioned Directives. In addition, the Commission currently assesses whether the EU OSH legal framework remains fit for purpose, and plans to adopt in 2026 a new European framework to strengthen resilience to, and management of, climate change related risks7.

Furthermore, EU-OSHA published the guide ‘Heat at Work – Guidance for Workplaces’8 as well as the Online Interactive Risk Assessment Tool (OiRA) ‘Heat and cold’9. In addition, the European Climate and Health Observatory provides information on the impacts of heat on the health, wellbeing and productivity of workers.
